query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small-volume, finely distributed ductile copper network via melt infiltration into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy will reinforce the brittle caloric material to yield robust mechanical integrity without degrading its caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy that displays a large caloric effect under applied-field and pressure-field cycling but suffers from poor mechanical integrity and crack propagation.
generation.intervention: Melt infiltrate the porous or pre‐patterned (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 body with a controlled, low volume fraction (e.g., 10–20 vol%) of high-purity copper so that a bicontinuous composite structure is formed.
generation.conditions: The processing and subsequent testing are carried out under typical operating temperatures for the caloric transformation (near room temperature to the operating transformation temperature), under applied magnetic/pressure fields and moderate compressive loading; copper infiltration must be optimized to remain below about 30 vol% to avoid dilution of the caloric phase.
generation.structural_mediator: A bicontinuous microstructure in which the continuous, ductile copper network interpenetrates the caloric matrix, providing crack bridging and load transfer while maintaining intimate connectivity of the active caloric phase.
generation.mechanism: The copper network, owing to its ductility and high thermal conductivity, acts as a reinforcing scaffold that limits crack initiation and propagation and improves compressive strength. Simultaneously, because copper has high thermal conductivity and is introduced only in a limited fraction, it minimally interferes with the intrinsic caloric phase transformation, thus preserving the large caloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unchanged alloy, the copper-infiltrated composite should exhibit a significant increase in compressive strength (targeting values above ~200 MPa, similar to or exceeding those seen in epoxy‐modified samples) with marked suppression of crack formation, while the caloric effect (measured by isothermal entropy change or adiabatic temperature change under applied-field and pressure-field cycling) remains within approximately 10% of the original performance. Thermal conductivity is expected to increase, further aiding heat transport during caloric cycling.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which offers a large caloric effect but exhibits poor mechanical integrity (low compressive strength and a propensity to crack).
generation.boundary: The intervention is designed for use in the operating regime where the alloy’s caloric transformation occurs (near room temperature to moderate elevated temperatures under applied-field/pressure-field conditions) and under moderate compressive loads. Excess copper content (>30 vol%) or improper distribution could dilute the active caloric phase and compromise performance; thus, processing parameters must be carefully controlled.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal copper volume fraction, distribution, and processing parameters need experimental determination to balance mechanical reinforcement with the preservation of the caloric effect. The precise quantitative improvement in compressive strength and any minor impacts on caloric performance remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of copper-infiltrated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples with varying copper contents (e.g., 0%, 10%, 20%, and 30% by volume) using a controlled melt infiltration process. Perform compressive strength tests, caloric response measurements (such as isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change under the same applied-field/pressure-field conditions), and microstructural analyses (fractography and SEM) to assess crack propagation.
measurements: Compressive strength (in MPa) under standard uniaxial compression tests
Caloric response parameters (isothermal entropy change and/or adiabatic temperature change) under applied-field/pressure-field cycling
Microstructural imaging (SEM/EBSD) to evaluate the copper network distribution and crack suppression
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the copper-infiltrated composites do not show a significant improvement in compressive strength (i.e., do not reach or exceed ~200 MPa) and/or if the caloric response degrades by more than ~10% relative to the as-prepared alloy, the hypothesis will be rejected.
